Climate disasters know no boundaries. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Climate disasters do not stop at national borders, distinguish between rich and poor countries, or spare nations simply because their contribution to global greenhouse-gas emissions is small.
A changing climate is a shared global crisis, but its impacts are often felt most severely by countries that have contributed the least to the problem.
Nepal is a striking example of this injustice. According to the global emission reports, Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global carbon dioxide emissions. Yet the country remains highly vulnerable to climate-related disasters. The recent flash floods demonstrate how quickly extreme weather can turn into tragedy, destroying homes, infrastructure, and livelihoods.
The tragedy becomes even more compelling when Nepal's geography is considered. Home to some of the world's highest mountains, Nepal is part of the Himalayan region, an area sometimes described as the “ t hird p ole” because of its enormous stores of ice.
Nepal's glaciers have lost around one-third of their ice over three decades as global temperatures have risen. This transformation is not merely an environmental concern. It threatens water security, agriculture, ecosystems, settlements, and millions of people who depend on Himalayan rivers.
When glaciers melt more rapidly, the consequences can occur in stages. Initially, increased melting can contribute to greater water flows and create dangerous glacial lakes. These lakes can become unstable, potentially triggering sudden floods downstream.
At the same time, continued glacier loss threatens the long-term availability of water for communities and agriculture. Thus, what happens high in the mountains can eventually affect people far beyond the immediate glacier environment.
The recent flooding illustrates the human face of this crisis. V ideos show rescuers working through dangerous floodwaters to save people, including elderly and vulnerable residents. At least 579 people have been killed, with close to 2,000 missing. Behind these numbers are families separated from loved ones, homes swept away, communities struggling to recover, and people suddenly deprived of their livelihoods.
This is the fundamental injustice of climate change: T hose who contribute the least can suffer some of the greatest consequences.
For decades, industrialized economies have produced a disproportionately large share of historical greenhouse-gas emissions. According to the UNEP Emissions Gap Report 2025; the G20 group of the w orld’s 20 largest economies accounted for about 77% of global GHG emissions in 2024.
Meanwhile, countries such as Nepal and Bangladesh, which have made a comparatively tiny contribution to cumulative global emissions, face extraordinary exposure to climate-related hazards.
This imbalance raises an important question of climate justice: Who should bear the cost of this crisis?
Climate change is not simply an environmental issue. It is an issue of justice, development, poverty, human rights, and international responsibility.
A devastating flood in Nepal can destroy the progress that communities have achieved over decades. Roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms, and businesses can disappear within hours. For families living close to the poverty line, losing a house or livelihood can mean years of hardship.
The effects also extend beyond the immediate disaster zone. Floods can disrupt transportation, communication, electricity, and food supplies. Agricultural production may suffer, while damaged infrastructure increases the cost of reconstruction.
Governments in vulnerable countries are then forced to divert scarce resources from education, health, poverty reduction, and development towards emergency response and rebuilding.
Emissions from factories, power plants, vehicles, and other sources in one part of the world can influence climatic conditions thousands of kilometres away. A country cannot isolate itself from the consequences of global warming simply by reducing its own emissions.
But recognizing this interconnectedness must not become an excuse for inaction.
Every country has a responsibility to reduce emissions and strengthen climate resilience according to its capacity and circumstances. At the same time, countries that have contributed more significantly to historical emissions have a particular responsibility to support vulnerable nations around the world, especially South Asian countries.
For countries like Nepal, adaptation is essential. Communities need stronger early-warning systems, climate-resilient infrastructure, safer settlements, improved disaster preparedness, and effective emergency-response mechanisms. Mountain ecosystems require greater protection, and scientists need continued support to monitor glaciers, glacial lakes, and other indicators of environmental change.
However, adaptation alone cannot solve the problem. There is a limit to how much vulnerable countries can adapt if global temperatures continue to rise.
The lesson from Nepal should also resonate strongly across South Asia. Bangladesh, India, Bhutan, Pakistan, and other countries in the region face different but interconnected climate risks.
Floods, cyclones, landslides, droughts, heatwaves, river erosion, and changing rainfall patterns are already threatening communities across national borders. What happens in the Himalayas can influence river systems downstream. What happens in one country can create consequences for another.
This interconnected nature of climate risk requires interconnected solutions.
Governments must strengthen regional cooperation in disaster preparedness, weather forecasting, river management, and information sharing. International institutions like the United Nations must ensure that vulnerable countries receive meaningful financial and technical assistance. Climate finance should reach communities on the front lines of climate impacts rather than remaining trapped in complicated bureaucratic systems.
Most importantly, climate action must move beyond speeches and declarations. The people facing floods, storms, droughts, and disappearing glaciers cannot afford endless promises. They need practical action.
The images of rescuers carrying people from floodwaters are more than scenes of a natural disaster. They are a warning to the world.
Nepal's experience therefore demands that we rethink how we understand climate responsibility. A country's emissions may be small, but its vulnerability may be enormous.
Conversely, countries with greater historical emissions have a greater responsibility to lead the transition towards a low-carbon future and help those already suffering the consequences.
Climate change is global, but climate vulnerability is unequal. Borders may separate countries politically, but they cannot separate them from the atmosphere, oceans, rivers, and weather systems that connect our planet.
The time has come for the world to recognize that climate justice is not charity. It is a shared responsibility. If emissions produced in one part of the world can contribute to suffering in another, then climate action, financing, technology, and solidarity must cross borders as well.
Nepal's floods should not be viewed as an isolated national tragedy. They should be understood as a warning from a vulnerable country to the entire world: N o nation can escape a changing climate alone, and no country should be left to face its consequences alone.
Nicholas Biswas is a media freelancer and a recipient of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) Media Award. He can be reached at: gonomaddyom@gmail.com .

item.title: A helping hand from China. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The newly signed memorandum of understanding (MoU) between Bangladesh and China to expand cooperation in technical education and skills development is an excellent step, and one that aligns directly with one of our country’s most urgent development needs.
Bangladesh’s economy in recent years has been held back not by a lack of ambition, but by a shortage of skilled workers. In addition, despite calls for technical education needing more investment and attention, those calls have often fallen on deaf ears.
To that end, that Bangladesh and China will now cooperate in vocational training programs, bilingual educational materials, vocational education research, industry-education integration, industrial training in Bangladesh, study visits to China, and specialized training programs for vocational education, can only be seen as a positive step.
This agreement has the potential to begin strengthening the very foundation of our workforce. As the economy evolves - with growing opportunities in ICT, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, and other relevant sectors - the demand for technically-trained workers will only continue to rise. Yet too many young Bangladeshis still enter the job market without the skills employers need.
Partnerships like this can help close that gap. China has extensive experience in technical and vocational education, and Bangladesh stands to benefit from knowledge transfer, modern equipment, and updated training standards.
If implemented effectively, this cooperation can produce graduates who are more competitive, more employable, and better prepared for both domestic and international job markets.
Bangladesh cannot rely on low‑skill labour indefinitely. To move up the value chain, investing in people, especially the youth, is the only logical step. This MoU is therefore a welcome move, but it must be followed by sustained commitment.
Strengthening technical education is essential for building the Bangladesh of tomorrow. This is what must be recognized.

item.title: Enforced disappearances must never be allowed to return. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Today marks the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances.
With the 2026 theme of “Victims first. Actions now,” the United Nations rightfully call to place victims at the centre of all efforts and note that enforced disappearances are preventable and that it is nations and other stakeholders that have clear responsibilities and tools to act.
For our country, this day is of particular significance as we remember one of the darkest chapters of our recent history - a period when citizens could be taken without warrant, held without acknowledgement, and erased from public view.
For years, families here lived with unbearable uncertainty, not knowing whether their loved ones were alive or dead. Reports from human rights groups and UN investigators have documented patterns of abduction, secret detention centres, torture, and concealment carried out by state agencies during the previous regime.
The mass uprising of 2024 may have forced a reckoning, and Bangladesh has since taken steps toward reform, including drafting new legislation to criminalize enforced disappearance and strengthen accountability mechanisms.
With that said, it is evident from our recent history that laws alone are not enough. Rights organizations have warned that without institutional reform, independent oversight, and political commitment, the culture of impunity could persist, and enforced disappearances could once again make a comeback.
Bangladesh owes its citizens truth and justice. Protecting these rights is not only a legal obligation but a moral one, essential to rebuilding trust and ensuring that the state serves its people.
This day must therefore serve as a national reminder: Never again. Never again should families be forced to search for answers in silence and fear. Never again should any government be allowed to use disappearance as a tool of repression and control.

item.title: All roads lead to productivity. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
To introduce you to Venning's Law: the correct answer to any question containing the word “surely” is “no.” This is one of the lesser known laws about how the world works. It's even one of those I might be responsible for -- this explains why it isn't well known.
John Venning taught me English at school and then went on to become merely the head of English at one of the best schools in England -- as you can see, that career arc peaked early with that possibility of educating me.
The law came from just a passing remark in a class one day. But it has stuck with me and I've now been repeating it for decades. Anyone saying “but, surely” is avoiding having to make their case and is instead trying to insist that it's just obvious.
Which brings me to this, in this newspaper : “Even so, productivity isn’t the only thing that we care about, surely.” And the answer is, well, yes it is. That is, the claim that we care about other things is untrue, the answer to that question is “no.”
Now we do need to be careful here. Of course we care about other things than productivity -- a baby's smile is worth more than most of what we all do at work after all. But when we consider work, then yes, we really do care about productivity. To the near exclusion of everything else.
As Paul Krugman -- and he does, after all, have a Nobel in this subject of economics -- has pointed out, productivity isn't everything. But in the long run it's pretty much everything.
To take a step back into the real economic basics. Everything that is produced is consumed. The price of everything that is bought becomes an income to someone.
This is just the truth. For we define it that way when we work out gross domestic product, ie, GDP. Production equals income equals consumption. We've just defined it that way at the start so it must be true.
Which means that the average wage in a country, in an economy, is defined by the average amount that each worker produces -- the productivity of labour. How much we can each consume depends upon how much each of us can and do produce -- another point that Krugman is known to make.
How much we each produce in our work is the productivity of our labour. That's a definition, one of those things that simply is true because that's where we started from. So, yes, we really do care about productivity. Because that's what defines our living standards.
Higher productivity means higher wages, means higher consumption. For the obvious reason that if we produce more per hour we work, then we can consume more for each hour that we work.
Which is the same statement that our incomes are higher -- we have agreed that this last point is true simply because that's how we defined it all at the start.
Now, Becca Clarke -- the author of the original article -- is a postdoctoral fellow at the London School of Economics, the same university I learned my economics at. She's a lot further up the academic ladder than I ever got.
But it's still true that she is, here, wildly wrong. Because as far as work is concerned, then, yes, productivity is, in the long run, just about the only thing we care about.
She wants to talk about gender equality and other such things. Work/life balance, making a better society, and all that sort of stuff. Which is great -- I'm all in favour of a better life in that more rounded sense too.
The thing that economists keep pointing out is that all of those desirable things come from being rich. Getting rich means high productivity of labour. Because when we each produce more per hour -- and can then consume more per hour, have higher incomes per hour of our work -- then we can spend that higher income as we wish. Decide upon our own consumption. On such things as gender equality, for example.
The reason productivity really is pretty much the only thing we care about is that high productivity is exactly, specifically, what opens up that possibility of a better life more generally to us. It's also the only thing that does -- which is why, yes, really, that is pretty much the only thing we care about in the long term.
Oh, and yes, John Venning was right. Whenever anyone says “but, surely” they're glossing over the same gaping hole in their argument.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.
